Q26.text: I am very lucky in that I found a program that has been a really great fit for me, but there’s a certain lack of transparency between the mentor faculty and students that is the main frustration I have with the academic system at my university. For example, our first year is spent rotating through different labs until we decide which to do our dissertation work in. Faculty aren’t always honest about whether they have the funding to support students beyond the rotation and often use it as an excuse to not keep students they were unhappy with, rather than explaining what they didn’t find satisfactory about their work. One PI said “I didn’t get any students for two years after I told a student I didn’t think my lab was a good fit and they told others I was mean so now I just tell them I won’t have the money to pay their stipend so they choose not to stay”. I understand it’s a hard conversation to have but it’s rather disheartening to know that we can’t count on honest feedback when we’re here to be trained.

Q26.text: In the growing times of global scientific collaborations and diversification of the scientific talent pool, I am very shocked by the academic system. Having pursued both my Master's and PhD at reputed institutes and research groups in Germany, I have witnessed how there is nothing 'International' about the graduate programmes except for the students.  The lack of a proper support system for International students is a major let-down. Case in point, most PIs recruit international students knowing well about how visa extensions and working contracts go hand-in-hand. They then use this to exploit students, even threatening them to work without a work-life balance. Vacations are only sanctioned if  results as expected by the PI are available. More horrific, is the fact that Science is being carried out to please the PI's ego or a skewed vision of facts lending to publications of either cherry-picked data not entirely reflecting the complete scenario or simply 're-inventing the wheel'. And, to think of the tax-payers' money going down the drain for this rallies me up! Also, the utter lack of mentoring or interest in the graduate student's academic career or PhD experience (forget about future career prospects) has left me questioning my choices of an academic career.

Q26.text: 6 years in a PhD program. It is very varied and really depends on every individual PI and student. We can set the bar really low and say "yes the student graduated and also published a paper" but that is not good. Not all PhDs are also created equal. Some PhD students can graduate without publishing (field dependent), whereas some are expected to publish at least two first-author papers. But no worries, if the PhD students remain in the academic system, they can do 1 to 3 more postdocs in their 30s and earn an OK income that is on average lower than their counterparts who did not do a PhD. You could raise a small family on that income in some places that are not expensive. Don't worry about them not having retirement funds like a 401K. In my opinion, no one should do a PhD unless they don't have a better option in life. In the majority of cases, it is not a good experience and I don't recommend it to anyone.

Q26.text: Ate o momento, consigo  perceber que fazer um Doutorado em um pais com uma cultura extremamente diferente e que e automaticamente refletida na cultura educacional, e um desafio tremendo, que tem impacto direto na saude mental dos estudantes. Por exemplo, venho da cultura ocidental, onde hierarquias quase sao nulas (as relacoes sao bem horizontais); a autonomia, a proatividade e a liberdade no ambiente academica sao consideradas como qualidade e bem vistas pelos Professores; o equilibrio entre vida pessoal e profissional tambem sao bem vistos e devem co-existir. Entretanto, no Japao, a sociedade e extremamente hierarquizada e essa hierarquia e refletida fortemente no ambiente academico, onde os professores sao tomam uma posicao enorme de poder e respeito, colocando-os em uma posicao inacessivel ao estudante. E isso abre tambem precedentes gravissimos para a quase institucionalizacao do abuso moral e de poder (e, uma vez, que a hierarquia e sumariamente respeitada, esses episodios quase nao sao reportados por parte dos estudantes). Ainda, considerando esse posicionamento dos professores nessa hierarquia engessada, os estudantes nao sao bem vistos se questionam, apresentam personalidade e demandam discussao (a relacao e sempre muito de submissao e negacao de discussoes). E, por ultimo, o Japao e reconhecido como o lugar que as longas jornadas de trabalho 12-14 horas por dia sao bem vistas (nao import se isso leva a uma produtividade ou nao, se a pessoa esta sofrendo ou nao), o status valorizado aqui e quantas horas voce se mantem no ambiente de trabalho e anule a sua vida pessoal. Desse modo, a ciencia aqui, que demanda debate, discussao, opinioes e completamente negada pelo sistema hierarquico, bem como sao valorizados os estudantes que vao se degradando fisicamente ao longo do seu Doutorado. Adicionalmente, o Japao e um pais, extremamente xenofobico e, enquanto estudante internacional, esse preconceito e sentido em cada detalhe da vida academica, onde, nao importa o que voce faca, atinja ou demonstre: no final e cada esquina, voce sera sumariamente desacreditado, descredibilizado e desencorajado. E, toda essa situacao nao se aplica a mim, se estende a todos os outros estudantes internacionais que aqui convivo. E algo realmente muito grave e dificil de mudar.

Q16.text: A potencialidade da minha pesquisa ser muito menos explorada e ser fadada a menores alcances (achievements) ao considerar todo o abandono, a falta de interesse e o desapoio do meu Orientador de Doutorado (das coisas mais tristes e angustiantes que tenho enfrentado nesse Doutorado). No Brasil, sempre trabalhei com infra-estrutura e recursos escassos, mas eu tive grandes Professores, que me orientavam, eram modelos de inspiracao como seres humanos e profissionais para mim (foram eles,  sem duvida alguma, o maior fator de eu ter escolhido a carreira academica). Desse modo, mesmo com recursos fisicos escassos, eu tive a chance de atingir grandes resultados, porque tinha grandes professores por tras de mim. Entretanto, apos ter convivido com 4 grandes professores-orientadores que muito me ensinaram, durante o meu Bacheralado e Mestrado, desde que iniciei meu Doutorado no Japao, tenho sofrido claramente o completo abandono, desinteresse, falta de motivacao/liberdade e, aparentemente, falta de conhecimento solidos para dar suporte a minha pesquisa por parte do meu Orientador. Q26.text: First of all, in the Netherlands, bright people are leaving academia due to the lack of grants. It is very hard to pursue an academic career when you stay in the Netherlands. Therefore, I moved to the USA to follow working in academia as a postdoctoral researcher, and I hope that this experience will give me (some) advantage in grant applications when I move back to the Netherlands in 3-4 year.   Secondly, although i started working as a postdoctoral researcher here in the USA, I am still finishing my PhD program, due to the Dutch system. As molecular cell biologists, we need to have 2 published papers and a third submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, before you can finish your thesis and set a date for a defense. Since publishing has become harder over the years (more data needed, extensive peer-review cycles that are both very consuming when the manuscript is rejected after review and needs to be submitted elsewhere where the whole cycle will start again), I have not been able to finish my PhD in the time set to do so. I started as a PhD-student in August 2013 and was supposed to finish in 4 years. Then, I was extended with one year and I left for a postdoc in Augstus 2018. To date, June 2019, I'm still not finished since manuscript acceptance takes too long.   I was lucky that my new PI here in the USA was understanding that defense in the Netherlands depends on publications, but officially I am not working as a postdoc now, but as a research specialist on a postdoc project. I know of a lot of Dutch colleagues that had to let go of their dream of a postdoc in the USA, because of this problem.  I think it is unfavorable that PhD programs differ so much between countries. Q26.text: Academia can be a great place to be - its a unique environment that can be relaxed and creative. Ultimately though, academia is geared towards giving power and a sense of entitlement to PIs, and has lost sight of its responsibilities regarding student wellbeing. Universities have given such power and status to PIs that they can't even control them anymore. PIs don't respect university/HR systems and standard work place etiquette.    A lovely example of academia failings: I collaborate with industry and have 1 university PI and 2 industrial PIs. I have had my industrial PI make inappropriate comments to me ranging from sexual harassment to being purely nasty. One example to give you a flavour: whats happened to your skin? how do you expect to be taken seriously when you look like a spotty teenager - you should really cover your spots up. I raised this with my uni PI and described other events that had made me uncomfortable and it was shrugged off as typical behaviour from this industrial PI. the take home message was basically that we gain funding and resource from the collaboration so leave it. At this point I had had a diagnosed breakdown after a very rough first year, so was in no position to argue. As a PhD student you sometimes forget that you're a person who is entitled to opinions and feelings.  Academia needs a huge shake up (a big old slap really!), from the top down.

Q26.text: The academic system is designed to train PhD students to become PIs. In the process of doing so, PhD students gain valuable experience and transferable skills that make them competent and resourceful individuals. However, the expectation is very much that you would continue on to a post-doc position. This, in my view, is not a good thing given the relatively few academic jobs available. PhD programmes should establish closer links to industry and and other non-research related science careers to ensure that PhD students gain the skills aligned with these careers after they graduate, and build networks to facilitate job opportunities. PhD programmes and institutions also do not articulate well enough the capabilities of PhD graduates to employers in the wider sector, and can improve on this.  PIs and funding bodies have a lot of incentive to employ PhD students and post-docs in the short term on temporary contracts, but the academic system should incentivise instead the hiring of permanent staff scientists for those who want to be in the lab full-time. For those that don't, greater exposure to other career paths (eg. talks, networking opportunities, work experience placements and internships) is needed for PhD students' career progression.  In many cases, poor supervision from the PI and a negative group environment can detract from the PhD experience - this is really hard to judge from a short interview.

Q55.text: Have a good think about career paths and thoroughly explore opportunities before starting. Pick a PhD in a field with clear connections to industry and hireable skills, that also interests you. Spend more time in the first 1/2 of the PhD deciding on career path, to plan an exit strategy about ~2y before graduation.

Q26.text: This system is designed to break people slowly, so they don't realize what's happening until we can't sleep through the night and we feel guilt for watching tv on the weekends just to have a small break. The professors at my school expect everyone to be as dedicated as they are, but they have healthy salaries and good health insurance with families who can help them. Most of the grad students here are living in unhealthy situations. I am currently living in a house with termites and roaches 10 miles away from campus because it's all I can afford. My advisor quit her job as a professor and left me with no funding for my final semester of grad school, plus she has been a poor advisor overall because she is consistently underprepared, late, or distracted. I do not feel like a priority to her. Moreover, as an early career researcher herself, she doesn't have much experience or knowledge of opportunities even within academia, much less outside of it. Q26.text: The academic system needs a drastic overhaul. It has become a corrupt and abusive system. I would like to see major reforms at every single level. Most research is published for the sole reason of publishing a paper. Papers and impact factors have become the currency of academia; the desire to do Science for the sake of progress or humanity is largely non-existent. Most places and people care about the length of the CV, but no thought is spared towards the impact these studies may have had. Further, the Ph.D. student is left at the mercy of the supervisor and the academic system which tends to protect itself when questioned. Universities have become brands and they care too much about their brands. Harassment cases are quietly stamped out to protect the university's and the supervisor's reputation. This is true more so for international students who put their entire careers and lives on the line to work towards their Ph.D.s on a pittance. Lip service is paid to women empowerment, but women are consistently left out at every possible turn. A strong teaching effort is drummed up by universities, but everyone knows teaching takes away from one's ability to manufacture papers. It looks incredibly bleak for academia unless one is well-connected and comes with the right brand and backing. The way I see it, academia has stagnated and it does not look like things are changing for the better any time soon. Of course, one can write an entire article, and many have been written without much effect, about the publication system and the exorbitant cost of acquiring "knowledge" in today's world.

Q16.text: I find it absolutely baffling that academia, while propped up as the last bastion of ethical and moral purity, tolerates faculty and students with alarming behavioral issues. In my experience, I have seen faculty members get away with sexual harassment and abuse at multiple universities with supreme confidence. Further, the biggest lesson I have received during my Ph.D. is that academia rarely cares about merit or quality. There are, to the best of my knowledge, only two ways to get ahead: my advisor is well connected and/or I somehow manage to find my way onto a Nature or Science publication. Maybe this is to be expected given the shortage of jobs, but it makes academia an ideal breeding ground for abusive relationships. I also find that enough is not done to make incoming students understand how slim the chances of an academic career really are, post Ph.D. Maybe it is too much, and not even the point of a Ph.D., to train students for careers outside of academia. However, the system is nothing short of a scam if incoming students are, at the very least, not made aware of the reality of the job market. Precious few universities and departments actively expose their students to opportunities outside of academia by encouraging participation in workshops, conventions, presentations, alumni networks, etc. And no, it is not the sole responsibility of the incoming student to know how the job market is. It is similar to arguing that sweatshops employing immigrants in the Middle Eastern countries carry none of the blame and arguing instead that the blame must rest on the people working there "voluntarily".  And make no mistake, academia today is eerily similar to a sweatshop.

Q60.text: Yes! I entered my dissertation program focusing on research that bridges two different fields. In the beginning of my program, I was revered for that smart, forward-thinking twist to my research, and I was told repeatedly this is where the field needs to go (inter-disciplinary). Now, I am struggling to finish my dissertation, because every topic I suggest for my dissertation has been rejected by everyone in the department, since it is not traditionally within my field. And I never wanted this to happen to me, I had three options (I knew they were feasible, because another graduate student I worked with previously swiped one of those topics and graduated early and with praise) for dissertation topics as I entered the PhD program, because I knew I didn't want to be like other students I saw in my department that just appeared to take funding opportunities away from everyone while not progressing to graduation. Now I am that student. I even had a NSF DDIG proposal ready to submit (edits from the department lasted over 5 months, and it was ready!), and I was told they day of submission to our Office of Research, I should not submit, because no one in the department could supervise the project. I have since seen students AND professors independently come across those topics I have been steered away from, and those topics have been funded by major federal institutions, and the research yielded multiple publications in noteworthy journals. I am doing a dissertation project now that was not my idea, I have been handed the data, and it is my job just to analyze data that no one has used since the 1980's, just so I can graduate in 6 years. I know I sound like a complainer who is blaming everyone else for my problems. Maybe that is the case. I am saddened, because with those rejected topics have also gone my rose-colored glasses about the ability of research in academia to allow you to pursue passion projects. And even though my department publicly touts inter-disciplinary projects, there is no support for that in my department. It clearly took me too long for that to sink in.   Overall, I wish I had a mentor explain those hard facts to me; I wish I was smart enough to read between the lines to see inter-disciplinary research is not what my department produces; and I wish it did not have to be that way. Now, I just hope to graduate (later than I intended and with a project I am not sure contributes to modern society in any way), find an academic job (seemingly a one-in-a-million chance), and work to support inter-disciplinary research every day of my life.

Q26.text: Academic system is very bureaucratic and professors spend too much time in teaching and administrative duties. Since I like doing research, this discouraged me to pursue a professorship. There is a lack of full-time/tenured researchers who can provide solid advice on research methods and practice. Professors mostly don't do research themselves, besides quickly reviewing papers or thesis. This was a huge disappointment for me, because I thought I would have a strong and deep mentorship on research practice in the university setting.  The publish-or \-perish mentality is also a waste of the little time professors and postdocs have. This mentality makes people push for half-backed research results  (or hyped buzzwords) in order to increase publication count (or be present at a conference). The result (in my field at least) is a flood of low quality papers that are 90% written by students. This low quality takes enormous time from reviewers and makes conferences boring as participants barely ask questions or discuss the topics. Instead, I feel that most people are mostly interested in seeing and being seen.

Q60.text: When the survey questions uses the term "programme", it makes me assume that there should be a structure in the PhD graduate studies. I don't believe there is a structure, and I am not sure that it is possible or desirable to have one. Graduate school is not like the undergraduate school. While the undergrad school looks like a production of line of professionals, the graduate school experience is more of a one-to-one coaching. Therefore, "programme" could be a misleading term. I would not like to be in a strict standardized PhD program. I would rather have access to senior researchers who would actively advise me in various topics.   Now, we face the worst of the two worlds. US PhD programs are littered with artificial barriers, e.g., required lectures, required exams, required publications, required teaching assistant practice, etc). Meanwhile, these programs do not provide access to senior researchers (only to busy professors who don't practice research themselves because they are overloaded with lectures and administrative duties).   I think the survey should have also explored the topic of conferences and workshops. Conferences and workshops are sometimes advocated as events for students to get feedback. However, they are overcrowded, professors are busy meeting other professors, and people barely ask questions after the talks. The exception was the Doctoral Symposiums, where PhD Students get feedback on their research from a panel o professors. This was a great experience that I have in more than one conference.  The survey could have addressed bullying more deeply. As a graduate student, I saw the bullying of colleagues as the most serious issue in the university that I attended (UC Irvine). I would like to see more awareness and discussion about that. Is bullying cultural? Or is it a consequence of excessive competition in the US academic system?

In my case, I can't complain as much given that apart from working long hours and some things not going as you expected, I have been lucky with my supervisors which have always looked for a way to pay me a salary and fund the projects for my PhD thesis. Regarding my University, I only have contact with it when I have to pay the enrollment fees each year and visit the evaluation board that follows what I have been doing during that year (a 5-minute meeting). I do not receive any specific training but they do offer some seminars that you can attend to if you have the time (which is never).   As I said, although my experience has been good, I do consider that overall doing a PhD is not well valued nor recognized as one of the highest degrees, if not the highest. We are well trained and educated people with careers, masters and lots of experience. Although we are overqualified, we are normally underpaid and work extra hours, not only at the lab/office but also at home. This includes weekends. Therefore, the "underpayment" increases while your life balance decreases. Moreover, none of this assures you a stable, successful or any kind of future which is very unsettling and makes you kind of want to be a PhD student the rest of your life. Not sure this is an academic system issue alone but it is clear that the number of PhD student keeps increasing, and the present and future working conditions do not increase with it.

Q26.text: I find the academic system flawed and the concept of the positions outdated. In my mind, you should not be catagorized on each degree or position you complete, but evaluated by seniority and experience like on the job market. A person who gets a big dataset can get loads of results and publish easily while a person doing basic science has to work for years in calibrating and optimizing to get readable results.

Q26.text: Unstructured and stochastic with some labs/research groups that provide a lot of guidance for PhD students and others that leave PhD students completely alone and unsupervised. Inequality of resources and support (intellectual and financial), huge administrative load and impossible bureaucracy that strongly affect the quality of research. Doing a good PhD seems to be a lottery determined more on many external factors than on the students’ skills. Wrong evaluation criteria that do not take into account the student’s personal abilities and history but are just “performance-based” (publications number vs actual learning). A PhD seems more like a job for already advanced researchers to show what they can produce rather than a scientific training period for students to consolidate knowledge and learn new skills.

The academic system that we follow was set up with the right ethos. But in the execution we have all collectively faltered. It was one field of work which accommodated heterogeneity and diversity in all forms especially ideas and way of life but increasingly the system is trying to homogenize people making them loose their individuality. In older studies, journals reviewed and argued the science behind what the authors did, but now they review and make authors add more experiments which they want to see not necessarily needed for proving what the authors did. If big data is the current trend every research group is expected to have omics in their paper.  There is also this wave of applied research which as a standalone field is very good but inadvertently penetrates into basic research. All research cannot be applied immediately. Lots of drugs that are there in the market exist because their mechanism of action was a phenomenon some graduate student/post doc uncovered which could eventually get targeted. The original study may not even have proposed it. This also encourages researchers to portray hypothetical forced biomedical applications of their research findings and mislead people  when actually there may be none.  I also feel the system inherently assumes that people in academia don't have a life beyond work. They reinforce this assumption in their expectations from students and PIs. In fact its almost considered unusual if you are single and want to leave for home at decent hours after work. Family is the qualifier you need to enjoy time after work. This notion is largely in India. There are other inherent assumptions too like people doing science should look shabby and unkempt. This portrayal of scientists has become like a norm and if you don't fit into their mold you are not considered a serious scientist. People who are well dressed, especially women therefore have a hard time being taken seriously.

Q26.text: The academic system is quite flawed in my opinion. Most of the classes I had to take in my first year were useless and interfered with time I could have better spent in the lab. Important skills that would have benefited most students in my graduate studies (e.g. statistical knowledge) were never even touched on.  I had a very bad relationship with my first PI and my department had no way of knowing until I brought it to their attention. As I had never been a graduate student, I thought the situation was normal until I started discussing it with other students. By the time I realized what a toxic situation it was, I had already spent 3 years on the project. Furthermore, after running into some former students by chance, I learned that I wasn't the first student to be treated this way. This suggests that there are PIs out there who have a history of treating students unfairly but basically it is either swept under the rug by the department or never even brought to the attention of the department. I was definitely scared to speak out as my PI hinted that her recommendation would be the most important thing in my future. As far as I know, she is still a PI in the department and still accepting students. Even though I did interview with the lab and spoke to the grad students alone, they did not tell me any of the problems in the lab. But looking back I probably wouldn't either because it might get back to the PI.  As well, almost all PIs are academic. This means that many have no advice or connections to help students who would like to pursue non-academic career paths. I definitely feel like I am on my own once I graduate.

Q16.text: I started my PhD in a different lab then the one I am in now. I had a very bad relationship with my previous PI and moved lab after 3 years. I had to completely change projects and as a result I am in the 6th year of my PhD and won't finish till at least my 7th or 8th year. With the low pay and high cost of living, I have many things 'on hold' until I graduate and can get a better paying job. The low pay and high stress and workload of an academic job is one reason I am not even considering continuing in academia. One large concern I have going into my future career is that I want to have children fairly soon after I graduate as I am already 30. It's hard to think about finishing a PhD, finding a job, and also having children before I am too old.  At present I can't even say for certain that I will find a good job or one I am interested in...all I know is lab-based research.

Q55.text: I wish I'd known that I could change departments when going from undergrad to grad studies. I thought since I did an undergraduate in biochemistry and I couldn't pursue a different graduate program. This limited the pool of PIs and projects I was looking into. I think this is probably common knowledge for many students but as my parents did no attend university, they had weren't able to guide me and prospective universities don't really advertise this.  I also wish I had known to look at the number of publications per year that my prospective PI was publishing. If there are very few, it could point to problems in the lab unless they are pursing lengthy studies (e.g. animal aging). Also are their postdocs in the lab? I now work in a lab with postdocs and having that extra mentoring is amazingly useful. I would now look for labs where the project I am placed on is ongoing and one-on-one mentoring/teaching is available - either from a postdoc or ideally, another graduate student who is passing the project on as they are about to graduate. My first project was leftover (and unpublished) from about 6 years before and hadn't been investigated since. This is a big problem because not only do you have no one to talk to but other labs could be close to publishing results that may make the previous work obsolete.

Q26.text: Garbage. While I've been lucky to have an excellent mentor and dedicated committee, the department and school I'm in offer at best little support for graduate students, and at worst, active attempts to sabotage those students. The default assumption is that a funded graduate student will teach all five years of their funding package, and the burden of responsibility of those teaching assignments has steadily increased over the five years of my PhD. For example, introductory lab teaching responsibilities have increased from 2 courses/week per TA to 3 courses/week per TA. This adds another 30 students' worth of grading to grading responsibilities, and another 5 hours per week between actual lab run time (3 hours), setup and cleanup (1 hour) and office hours (1 hour per lab session). This makes it impossible to confine teaching responsibilities to the 20 hours/week we're paid for (if you're spending 15 hours a week teaching, that leaves 5 hours a week to grade 90 lab reports. You try grading 90 lab reports in 5 hours. It doesn't happen--and that's not counting troubleshooting via email or addressing student concerns over email). Additionally, the number of trainings for teaching responsibilities we are expected to complete rises steadily every year, creating an unpredictable time commitment that varies from semester to semester. The end result is a burdensome, difficult to navigate system that means for most of the time you're working, you're doing teaching-related activities. Late in the programme, as I am, this can be deadly--you're faced with a choice of whether to assume debt for your last year or years or quit the programme due to simply not having time for research due to teaching responsibilities.  This wouldn't be so bad if those assignments were predictable and reliable, but they aren't. Colleagues haven't received their contract or their funding until well after the semester's actually started; I've been badgered for weeks by the financial services offices on campus because my tuition remission hasn't gone through in a timely manner. The actual wages do not reflect the cost of living. I am lucky because I receive a degree of financial support from my family, but medical and other kinds of debt among graduate students at my institution is common. I've been cycled through five separate teaching assignments before the semester started, with the administrators responsible indicating that I might not have one, even if my funding package guarantees it. Overall, it means there's a great deal of insecurity in funding even well into the programme and with a funding package.   There is no ability to unionize or organize for better working conditions. This university is in a right-to-work state, and the graduate student government, while claiming to be lobbying for better wages, is in effect toothless and has had no success in improving working conditions. With the expected ruling that graduate student workers are students first and workers second, there is little likelihood that this will change.

Q60.text: Please do something to change the culture around graduate school. We are used as disposable workers, with little support or assistance available, and power imbalances mean that if a faculty member wants you out, you're out. Mental health initiatives are laughable; seeing a therapist once a week treats symptoms, but the underlying cause is an unhealthy, exploitative environment in which students are entirely at the mercy of faculty and paid extremely poorly. It would be better to allocate that money to paying students better and improving working conditions, thus alleviating the prevalent economic anxiety  and mental illness from stress and overwork. Mental health support is a band-aid. It's better to have it than nothing at all, but it doesn't actually prevent the injury in the first place.
